statement: A PIT histogram that slopes steadily in one direction, with realized outcomes systematically falling on one side of the forecast distribution, indicates a location bias in the forecast distribution rather than a problem with its width.
explanation: A monotone sloped PIT histogram means outcomes consistently land in the upper (or lower) part of the forecast distribution, so the forecast mean is off. Too-narrow forecasts give a U-shape and too-wide forecasts give a central hump instead.
originalText: The forecast distributions are biased in location: realized P&L is systematically higher than forecast, so the forecast is too pessimistic and the location (mean) should be adjusted.

statement: A concentration of PITs near 0 indicates that realized losses repeatedly fall in the extreme left tail of the forecast distribution, so large losses are underestimated.
explanation: A PIT is the forecast CDF evaluated at the realized P&L, so losses map to low values. A pile-up near 0 means losses land far in the forecast tail much more often than the model predicts.
originalText: The PIT distribution has a concentration of values near 0 (31% of PITs in the lowest decile versus 10% expected), indicating frequent underestimation of large losses.

statement: A PIT distribution that is uniform on the interval from 0 to 1, with no clustering in the tails or the centre, indicates that a VaR model is poorly calibrated.
explanation: Uniform PITs are the hallmark of a well-calibrated forecast distribution. Clustering in the tails or centre, not its absence, signals miscalibration.
originalText: The PIT distribution is uniform on \[0,1\], with no clustering in the tails or center.
correction: A PIT distribution that is uniform on the interval from 0 to 1, with no clustering in the tails or the centre, indicates that a VaR model is well calibrated.

statement: Well-calibrated PITs should have skewness near 0 and kurtosis near 3.
explanation: Skewness 0 and kurtosis 3 are the moments of a normal distribution. Well-calibrated PITs are uniform on the interval 0 to 1, which has skewness 0 and kurtosis of 1.8.
originalText: The PIT distribution has skewness near 0 and kurtosis near 3, indicating balanced calibration.
correction: Well-calibrated PITs should have skewness near 0 and kurtosis near 1.8.

statement: When backtesting VaR models, a QQ plot of PITs should ideally be close to a straight line from (0,0) to (1,1).
explanation: If PITs are uniform, the fraction of PITs at or below each value u equals u, which plots as the 45-degree line from (0,0) to (1,1). Deviations from that line show the forecast distribution is mis-specified.
originalText: straight line from \[0,0\] to \[1,1\].

statement: When backtesting VaR models, a QQ plot of PITs should ideally be close to a horizontal line.
explanation: A horizontal line would mean all PITs sit in one region, an extreme departure from uniformity. Uniform PITs give the 45-degree line from (0,0) to (1,1).
originalText: horizontal line.
correction: When backtesting VaR models, a QQ plot of PITs should ideally be close to a straight line from (0,0) to (1,1).

statement: For a perfect distribution forecast, each of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Anderson-Darling and Cramér-von Mises statistics is expected to converge toward zero as the number of observations grows.
explanation: All three statistics measure the distance between the empirical PIT distribution and the uniform distribution. With a perfect forecast the PITs are truly uniform, so the distance shrinks toward zero and lower values are better.
originalText: For a perfect distribution forecast, each of the KS, Anderson‑Darling and Cramér‑von Mises statistics is expected to converge toward zero as the number of observations grows.

statement: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is the mean squared deviation between the actual and theoretical distributions.
explanation: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is the maximum vertical distance between the actual and theoretical distributions. The Cramér-von Mises statistic is the one based on the mean squared deviation.
originalText: The KS statistic is the mean squared deviation between the actual and theoretical distributions, while the Cramér‑von Mises statistic is the maximum vertical distance.
correction: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is the maximum vertical distance between the actual and theoretical distributions.

statement: The Anderson-Darling test treats all discrepancies between the actual and theoretical distributions equally.
explanation: It is the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test that treats all discrepancies equally. The Anderson-Darling test places higher emphasis on the tails, which is why it is preferred for risk management.
originalText: The Anderson‑Darling test treats all discrepancies between the distributions equally, which is why it is preferred over KS for risk management.
correction: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test treats all discrepancies between the actual and theoretical distributions equally.

statement: A goodness-of-fit statistic that is larger than zero but below its critical value shows that the PITs are exactly uniform.
explanation: Being below the critical value only means uniformity is not rejected at that confidence level. It does not prove the PITs are exactly uniform.
originalText: A statistic that is larger than zero but below its critical value means the PITs are exactly uniform.
correction: A goodness-of-fit statistic that is larger than zero but below its critical value shows that uniformity of the PITs is not rejected.

changes.from: shows that the PITs are exactly uniform
changes.to: shows that uniformity of the PITs is not rejected

statement: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test measures the maximum vertical distance between the actual and theoretical distributions but treats all discrepancies equally, so it gives no extra weight to the tails.
explanation: KS takes the largest gap between the empirical and uniform CDFs wherever it occurs, so tail discrepancies get no special weight. This is the criticism that motivates the Anderson-Darling test.
originalText: It measures the maximum vertical distance between the actual and theoretical distributions but treats all discrepancies equally, so it gives no extra weight to the tails.

statement: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test is the most sensitive of the three tests to deviations in the tails of the distribution.
explanation: The Anderson-Darling test, not KS, places the heaviest emphasis on the tails. KS treats all discrepancies equally.
originalText: It is the most sensitive of the three tests to deviations in the tails of the distribution.
correction: The Anderson-Darling test is the most sensitive of the three tests to deviations in the tails of the distribution.

statement: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test averages squared deviations over the whole distribution.
explanation: Averaging squared deviations over the whole distribution describes the Cramér-von Mises statistic. KS uses the single maximum vertical distance between the distributions.
originalText: It averages squared deviations over the whole distribution and therefore cannot detect a single large deviation.
correction: The Cramér-von Mises test averages squared deviations over the whole distribution.

statement: The Cramér-von Mises test is very similar to the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test but, instead of the maximum difference, it considers the mean squared deviation between the distributions.
explanation: Both tests compare the empirical PIT distribution with the uniform distribution. Cramér-von Mises replaces the maximum gap with the mean squared deviation, so it assesses fit across the whole distribution.
originalText: CvM is very similar to KS but, instead of the maximum difference, it considers the mean squared deviation between the distributions.

statement: Among the Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Cramér-von Mises and Anderson-Darling tests, the Cramér-von Mises test places the greatest emphasis on tail observations.
explanation: The Anderson-Darling test, not Cramér-von Mises, emphasises tail observations. Cramér-von Mises averages squared deviations across the whole distribution.
originalText: CvM is the test with the greatest emphasis on tail observations among the three.
correction: Among the Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Cramér-von Mises and Anderson-Darling tests, the Anderson-Darling test places the greatest emphasis on tail observations.

statement: The Cramér-von Mises test tests the independence of successive PIT values rather than their distribution.
explanation: Cramér-von Mises is a goodness-of-fit test of whether PITs follow the uniform distribution. Independence is tested separately, for example with the Berkowitz approach on normal-transformed PITs.
originalText: CvM tests the independence of successive PIT values rather than their distribution.

statement: The Kupiec test evaluates the full distribution of PITs.
explanation: The Kupiec test looks only at the frequency of VaR exceedances. It does not examine the shape of the PIT distribution.
originalText: Kupiec test, because it evaluates the full distribution of PITs.
correction: The Kupiec test evaluates only the frequency of VaR exceedances.

changes.to: only the frequency of VaR exceedances

statement: A Cramér-von Mises test that does not reject uniformity proves that a VaR model is well calibrated in the tails.
explanation: Cramér-von Mises averages deviations across the whole distribution, so passing it says nothing reliable about the tails. A tail-sensitive test such as Anderson-Darling can still reject.
originalText: The Cramér‑von Mises test proves the model is well calibrated in the tails.

statement: Large Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramér-von Mises statistics with very small p-values indicate that the PITs closely fit the uniform distribution.
explanation: Large statistics and tiny p-values mean a large deviation from uniformity and a rejection of the null that PITs are uniform. A good fit shows small statistics and high p-values.
originalText: Model Y passes both tests, because its large test statistics indicate a close fit to the uniform distribution.
correction: Large Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramér-von Mises statistics with very small p-values indicate that the PITs deviate substantially from the uniform distribution.

statement: Among the goodness-of-fit tests used to evaluate the distribution of PITs, the Anderson-Darling test best captures tail events.
explanation: The Anderson-Darling statistic places higher emphasis on tail observations. KS looks only at the single largest gap and Cramér-von Mises averages squared deviations equally across the distribution.
originalText: Anderson‑Darling test.

statement: A low one-period autocorrelation of the average correlation series indicates a high mean reversion rate (gravity).
explanation: In the mean-reversion regression the autocorrelation equals one minus the mean reversion rate, so a low autocorrelation means a high mean reversion rate.
originalText: The mean reversion rate (aka, gravity) is high

statement: With mean reversion, the slope coefficient in the regression of the change in correlation on the lagged correlation level is positive.
explanation: The slope equals minus the mean reversion rate, so it is negative when correlation reverts to its mean.
originalText: The regression coefficient is positive
correction: With mean reversion, the slope coefficient in the regression of the change in correlation on the lagged correlation level is negative.

statement: The Johnson SB distribution is the best fit to the empirical distribution of equity correlations.
explanation: Johnson SB is a flexible bounded distribution that matches equity correlations well across economic states, whereas normal, lognormal and beta fit poorly.
originalText: Johnson SB

statement: The generalized extreme value distribution is the best fit to the empirical distribution of equity correlations.
explanation: The generalized extreme value distribution is the best fit for bond correlations. Equity correlations are best fit by Johnson SB.
originalText: Generalized extreme value
correction: The Johnson SB distribution is the best fit to the empirical distribution of equity correlations.

statement: Default probability correlations are best modeled using the Johnson SB distribution, whereas bond correlations are best modeled using the generalized extreme value distribution.
explanation: Default probability correlations behave like equity correlations and are best fit by Johnson SB. Bond correlations are best fit by the generalized extreme value distribution, with the normal also fitting well.
originalText: The default probability correlation distribution is best modeled using the Johnson SB distribution, whereas the bond correlation distribution is best modeled using the generalized extreme value distribution.

statement: Default probability correlations and bond correlations are both best modeled using the Johnson SB distribution.
explanation: Only default probability correlations (like equity correlations) are best fit by Johnson SB. Bond correlations are best fit by the generalized extreme value distribution.
originalText: Both the default probability correlation distribution and the bond correlation distribution are best modeled using the Johnson SB distribution.

statement: The best-fit distributions for equity, bond and default probability correlations are Johnson SB, generalized extreme value and Johnson SB, respectively.
explanation: Equity and default probability correlations share the Johnson SB best fit. Bond correlations are best fit by the generalized extreme value distribution, with the normal as a secondary fit.
originalText: Johnson SB, generalized extreme value, and Johnson SB.

statement: A DV01-neutral hedge assumes that yield changes are parallel across maturities, which is rarely the case in practice.
explanation: DV01 neutrality presumes the position and the hedging instrument have the same basis-point yield change. Real yield changes differ across maturities, so the hedge is imprecise.
originalText: It assumes yield changes are parallel across maturities, which is rarely the case.

statement: A DV01-neutral hedge captures non-parallel yield curve shifts across multiple bond maturities.
explanation: A DV01-neutral hedge cannot capture non-parallel shifts. That is one of its main weaknesses.
originalText: It captures non‑parallel yield curve shifts across multiple bond maturities.
correction: A DV01-neutral hedge cannot capture non-parallel yield curve shifts across multiple bond maturities.

statement: A DV01-neutral hedge neutralizes spread-related risks in addition to interest rate (yield) risk.
explanation: A DV01-neutral hedge addresses only yield (rate) risk. Spread and other risks remain in the position.
originalText: The strategy inherently assumes that all spread‑related risks are neutralized.

statement: A DV01-neutral hedge assumes that the yields on the position and on the hedging instrument change by the same number of basis points, whereas actual changes can be proportionally larger or smaller and dispersed.
explanation: The DV01 hedge hard-wires a one-for-one yield change. When actual yield changes differ in size or are dispersed, the hedge is imprecise.
originalText: It assumes the yields on the position and the hedging instrument change by the same number of basis points, whereas the actual changes can be proportionally larger or smaller and dispersed.

statement: A DV01-neutral hedge requires estimating a regression of historical yield changes.
explanation: A DV01-neutral hedge uses no historical data. It is the regression hedge that estimates a regression of yield changes, which can be unstable over time.
originalText: It requires estimating a regression of historical yield changes, which may be unstable over time.
correction: A regression hedge requires estimating a regression of historical yield changes.

statement: A DV01-neutral hedge accounts for convexity.
explanation: DV01 is a first-order measure of price sensitivity and ignores convexity. It includes no convexity adjustment.
originalText: It accounts for convexity and so over‑hedges when yields change by large amounts.
correction: A DV01-neutral hedge does not account for convexity.

statement: When a trader is concerned about the dispersion of the change in the nominal yield for a given change in the real yield, the DV01 hedge is the least effective hedging methodology, because it hard-wires a one-for-one yield change.
explanation: Regression and principal components hedges are calibrated to the observed relationships between yield changes. The DV01 hedge alone assumes both yields change by the same number of basis points.
originalText: DV01 hedge.

statement: A DV01-neutral hedge of a nominal Treasury bond with TIPS assumes that the nominal yield and the real yield change by the same number of basis points.
explanation: This one-for-one assumption is the main drawback, because nominal and real yields do not move one-for-one in practice, so the hedge is imprecise.
originalText: It assumes the nominal yield and the real yield change by the same number of basis points, whereas empirically the nominal yield tends to move by more than one basis point per basis point of real‑yield change.

statement: A DV01-neutral hedge can only be applied when the bond and the hedging instrument have identical maturities.
explanation: DV01 hedges are routinely used with instruments of different maturities, such as hedging a nominal bond with TIPS. No identical-maturity restriction exists.
originalText: It can only be applied when the bond and the hedging instrument have identical maturities.

statement: A regression hedge improves on a DV01-neutral hedge by setting the hedge amount from the historical relationship between the two yield changes (the regression slope), rather than assuming a one-for-one move.
explanation: The regression hedge adjusts the DV01-neutral hedge by the historical slope beta of the exposure's yield changes on the hedge instrument's yield changes, so it reflects how the yields have actually co-moved.
originalText: It sets the hedge amount using the historical relationship between the two yield changes (the regression slope), rather than assuming a one‑for‑one move.

statement: A regression hedge eliminates basis risk completely, because the regression residual is forced to zero.
explanation: The residual, which is the basis risk, remains. The regression only minimises its variance, and the standard error measures it.
originalText: It eliminates basis risk completely, because the regression residual is forced to zero.

statement: In a single-variable regression hedge, the risk weight applied to the hedging instrument equals the regression slope coefficient beta from historical yield changes, which can differ from 1.0.
explanation: The DV01-neutral hedge is the special case with a risk weight of 1. The regression hedge scales the hedge by the estimated beta.
originalText: It equals the regression slope coefficient $\beta$ from historical yield changes, which can differ from 1.0.

statement: In a single-variable regression hedge, the risk weight applied to the hedging instrument equals the regression R-squared.
explanation: The risk weight is the regression slope coefficient beta. R-squared measures the share of variance explained and is not used to scale the hedge.
originalText: It equals the regression R‑squared, the proportion of variance explained.
correction: In a single-variable regression hedge, the risk weight applied to the hedging instrument equals the regression slope coefficient.

statement: Compared with a yield-based DV01 hedge, a regression hedge minimizes the variance of the hedged position's profit and loss over the historical sample used to estimate it.
explanation: Least squares chooses beta to minimise the sum of squared residuals, and the residual is the hedged position's P&L. The DV01 hedge makes no such minimisation.
originalText: The regression hedge minimizes the profit and loss (P&L) variance of the hedged position.

statement: A regression hedge is based on economic theory and future developments rather than on empirical analysis.
explanation: A regression hedge is empirical: it uses the historical relationship between yield changes. It is not theory- or forecast-based.
originalText: The regression hedge is based on economic theory and future developments rather than empirical analysis.
correction: A regression hedge is based on empirical analysis of historical yield changes rather than on economic theory and future developments.

changes.from: economic theory and future developments rather than on empirical analysis
changes.to: empirical analysis of historical yield changes rather than on economic theory and future developments

statement: A key advantage of a regression hedge is that it gives an estimate of the hedged portfolio's volatility over time.
explanation: The regression automatically yields a standard error. Multiplied by the position's DV01 it estimates the volatility of the hedged P&L.
originalText: It gives an estimate of the hedged portfolio’s volatility over time.

statement: A single-variable regression hedge assumes that the beta estimated from historical yield changes stays constant over the hedging horizon.
explanation: Using the historical beta going forward presumes a stable relationship between the two yield changes. In practice beta varies, so it should be estimated over several periods.
originalText: Beta is constant over time, so the historical estimate is assumed to hold over the hedging horizon.

statement: Principal component analysis decomposes yield curve changes into uncorrelated components ordered by the variance they explain, so a few components capture most of the term structure's volatility.
explanation: PCA turns correlated rate changes into uncorrelated principal components. A few of them describe most term structure risk, which greatly simplifies hedging.
originalText: It decomposes yield curve changes into uncorrelated components, ordered by the variance they explain, so a few components capture most of the term structure’s volatility.

statement: Principal component analysis assumes that all rates are perfectly correlated, so a single factor describes every rate change.
explanation: PCA estimates correlations from the data and does not assume perfect correlation. If rates were perfectly correlated only one component would exist.
originalText: It assumes that all rates are perfectly correlated, so a single factor describes every rate change.

statement: Principal component analysis guarantees that the slope of the yield curve stays constant, so hedge ratios never need updating.
explanation: PCA only describes how the curve has moved. Slope is itself one of the components, and it varies over time.
originalText: It guarantees that the slope of the yield curve stays constant, so hedge ratios never need updating.

statement: A principal components hedge computes the portfolio's exposure to the first few dominant principal components, such as level and slope, and chooses hedge positions that make the net exposure to each of them zero.
explanation: Neutralising the few dominant, uncorrelated components hedges the bulk of term structure risk without hedging every rate separately.
originalText: Compute the portfolio’s exposure to the first few (dominant) principal components, such as level and slope, and choose hedge positions that make the net exposure to each of them zero.

statement: A principal components hedge sets the hedge ratio equal to the beta from regressing the portfolio's yield changes on the hedging instrument's yield changes.
explanation: That describes a regression hedge, which uses one hedging instrument and a beta from historical yield changes. A PCA hedge zeroes exposure to the dominant principal components.
originalText: Regress the portfolio’s yield changes on the hedging instrument’s yield changes and set the hedge ratio equal to the regression beta.
correction: A regression hedge sets the hedge ratio equal to the beta from regressing the portfolio's yield changes on the hedging instrument's yield changes.

statement: A principal components hedge computes only the portfolio DV01 and offsets it with a single instrument, assuming that all rates move in parallel.
explanation: That describes a DV01 hedge, which covers only the level (parallel shift) factor. A PCA hedge also neutralises exposure to slope and other dominant components.
originalText: Compute only the portfolio DV01 and offset it with a single instrument, assuming all rates move in parallel.
correction: A DV01 hedge computes only the portfolio DV01 and offsets it with a single instrument, assuming that all rates move in parallel.

statement: A covariance matrix of 13 rates has 78 distinct covariances plus 13 variances, whereas the covariance matrix of the corresponding principal components is diagonal.
explanation: With 13 rates there are 13 x 12 / 2 = 78 distinct covariances. Principal components are uncorrelated, so their covariance matrix has only the variances on the diagonal.
originalText: The rate covariance matrix has 78 distinct covariances (plus 13 variances), whereas the PC covariance matrix is diagonal.

statement: Principal components are fundamental economic factors that the analyst specifies in advance, which is why names such as level, slope and short rate are assigned before the analysis is run.
explanation: Principal components are derived from the covariance structure of the rates. Labels such as level, slope and short rate are descriptive interpretations given after estimation.
originalText: The PCs are fundamental economic factors that the analyst specifies in advance, which is why the names level, slope and short rate are assigned before the analysis is run.

statement: Principal component analysis produces as many principal components as there are rates, but only a few are needed to characterize term structure fluctuations.
explanation: For 13 rates PCA gives 13 components, yet the first three explain almost all of the variance, so they suffice for hedging.
originalText: PCA produces 13 principal components, but only a few (here three) are needed to characterize term structure fluctuations.

statement: Principal component analysis provides a single empirical, multi-factor description of term structure behavior that can be applied across all bonds.
explanation: The same small set of factors describes all rates, unlike a regression hedge, which is tied to a few specific bonds.
originalText: PCA provides a single empirical, multi‑factor description of term structure behavior that can be applied across all bonds.

statement: The first three principal components of the term structure, for example level, slope and short rate, tend to explain 90% or more of interest rate volatility.
explanation: A few components capture the vast majority of term structure volatility, which is what makes PCA hedging practical.
originalText: The first three components (for example, level, slope and short rate) tend to explain 90% or more of interest rate volatility.

statement: In principal component analysis, the number of components needed grows roughly in proportion to the size of the portfolio, so for large portfolios a regression hedge becomes more practical.
explanation: A small, fixed number of components describes the term structure for any number of bonds. The required number of factors does not scale with portfolio size, which is an advantage of PCA.
originalText: The number of components needed grows roughly in proportion to the size of the portfolio, so for large portfolios a regression hedge becomes more practical.

statement: Because principal components are uncorrelated with each other, the variance of a rate equals the sum of the squared loadings on the principal components.
explanation: Principal components are orthogonal by construction, so variances add with no covariance terms. The volatility of a rate is the square root of the sum of its squared loadings.
originalText: Principal components are uncorrelated with each other, so the variance of a rate equals the sum of the squared loadings on the PCs.

statement: In a calibrated interest rate tree, a bond's current market price equals its expected discounted value computed with real-world probabilities.
explanation: The tree's probabilities are risk-neutral: they are the ones chosen so that the model price equals the observed market price. Real-world probabilities are not used for pricing in the tree.
originalText: The bond’s current market price of \$952.79 assumes real‑world probabilities applied to its expected discounted value (EDV)
correction: In a calibrated interest rate tree, a bond's current market price equals its expected discounted value computed with risk-neutral probabilities.

statement: Extending an interest rate tree to further dates requires assumptions about future short-rate values and risk-neutral probabilities that recover a given set of bond prices.
explanation: Each added date must be calibrated to the observed prices of additional bonds, so the new rates and probabilities have to reproduce them.
originalText: Extending the tree to further dates (e.g., 2 years, 2.5 years) requires assumptions about future short‑rate values and risk‑neutral probabilities that recover a given set of bond prices

statement: Compared with noncallable bonds, callable bonds have their capital gains capped as yields rise.
explanation: The issuer's call option caps price gains when yields fall, because the bond is likely to be called. When yields rise the call is far out of the money and the bond behaves like a noncallable bond.
originalText: Capital gains are capped as yields rise.
correction: Compared with noncallable bonds, callable bonds have their capital gains capped as yields fall.

statement: Callable bonds have less price volatility than otherwise identical noncallable bonds.
explanation: A callable bond is a noncallable bond minus an issuer call option. The short call dampens price moves, especially when yields are low.
originalText: They have less price volatility.

statement: Compared with noncallable bonds, callable bonds have negative convexity.
explanation: When yields are low the price is compressed toward the call price, so the price-yield curve flattens. That is negative convexity, whereas noncallable bonds are positively convex.
originalText: They have negative convexity.

statement: For callable bonds, reinvestment rate risk rises at low yields.
explanation: At low yields the issuer is likely to call, returning the call price plus coupon that must be reinvested at lower rates.
originalText: At low yields, reinvestment rate risk rises.

statement: If a security's market price is below its model value, its option-adjusted spread is positive and the security is trading cheap relative to the model.
explanation: A market price below model value requires a higher discount rate, so a positive constant spread must be added to the tree's short rates. A positive OAS corresponds to a cheap security.
originalText: The OAS is positive; the security is trading cheap relative to the model.

statement: If a security is not priced in accordance with the model (its OAS is not zero), its cash flows in the tree are discounted at the short-term rate plus the OAS.
explanation: The OAS is the constant spread added to every one-period discount rate in the tree so that model value equals market price.
originalText: The short‑term rate plus the OAS

statement: If a security's OAS is not zero, its cash flows in the tree are discounted at the short-term rate minus the OAS.
explanation: The OAS is added to the short rates. If the market price exceeds model value the OAS is simply negative.
originalText: The short‑term rate minus the OAS
correction: If a security's OAS is not zero, its cash flows in the tree are discounted at the short-term rate plus the OAS.

statement: When a bond's embedded options are removed, its option-adjusted spread reduces to the Z-spread, the constant spread over the spot curve that matches the bond's price.
explanation: Without optionality, interest rate paths no longer affect cash flows, so volatility is irrelevant and the OAS collapses to the zero-volatility spread.
originalText: Z‑spread

statement: An option-adjusted spread requires the security to have an embedded option.
explanation: OAS applies to any security valued on a tree, with or without an embedded option. It is the spread that equates the model value with the market price.
originalText: The OAS cannot be interpreted because this is a CMT swap, and an OAS requires an embedded option.
correction: An option-adjusted spread does not require the security to have an embedded option.

statement: A swap struck at the current rate and valued on a symmetric recombining rate tree with 50/50 probabilities need not be worth exactly zero, because discount factors are convex in the rate, so symmetric payments are discounted at different node rates and do not fully offset.
explanation: This is Jensen's inequality, the convexity effect of discounting. It arises even though the up and down moves and their probabilities are symmetric.
originalText: Convexity: discount factors are convex in the rate, so the symmetric payments are discounted at different node rates and do not offset (Jensen’s inequality)

statement: If all investors agree with certainty that the current one-year spot rate of 1.0% will rise to 2.0% next year and to 3.0% the year after, the three-year spot rate should be almost 2.0% with annual compounding.
explanation: The three-year spot rate is the geometric average of the expected one-year rates: (1.01 x 1.02 x 1.03) to the power 1/3 minus 1 is about 1.9967%.
originalText: If all investors agree with certainty that the current one‑year spot rate of 1.0% will increase to 2.0% next year and again to 3.0% in two years, the three‑year spot rate should be almost 2.0% (with annual compounding)

statement: Pure (strict) expectations theory cannot be expected to fully characterize the term structure in practice.
explanation: The actual curve also reflects risk premiums and convexity, which pure expectations theory ignores.
originalText: It is unreasonable and impractical to expect pure (and strict or narrow) expectations theory to fully characterize the term structure in practice

statement: Under pure expectations, a downward-sloping term structure implies that investors are forecasting a drop in future short-term interest rates.
explanation: With pure expectations, forward rates equal expected future spot rates, so a declining curve signals that lower short rates are expected.
originalText: Under an assumption of pure expectations, it is valid to hypothesize (infer) from a downward‑sloping term structure that investors are forecasting a drop in future short‑term (e.g., one year) interest rates

statement: If investors are risk neutral and agree on a binomial interest rate tree, higher volatility decreases yields and increases bond prices because of the convexity effect.
explanation: Bond prices are convex in rates, so by Jensen's inequality the expected discount factor exceeds the discount factor at the expected rate. A higher expected price means a lower yield, and the effect grows with volatility.
originalText: Higher volatility will decrease the yield and increase bond prices due to the convexity effect

statement: If investors are risk neutral and agree on a binomial interest rate tree, higher volatility increases yields and decreases bond prices because of the convexity effect.
explanation: The convexity effect raises expected bond prices and lowers yields. Higher yields would require a positive risk premium, which is absent here.
originalText: Higher volatility will increase the yield and decrease bond prices due to the convexity effect
correction: If investors are risk neutral and agree on a binomial interest rate tree, higher volatility decreases yields and increases bond prices because of the convexity effect.

changes.from: increases yields and decreases bond prices
changes.to: decreases yields and increases bond prices

statement: If investors are risk neutral and agree on a binomial interest rate tree, then with expected future short-term rates unchanged, greater interest rate volatility has no impact on the term structure.
explanation: Holding expected rates fixed does not neutralise volatility. Through Jensen's inequality the expected bond price rises, so spot rates fall.
originalText: If expected future short‑term interest rates are unchanged, greater interest rate volatility has no impact
correction: If investors are risk neutral and agree on a binomial interest rate tree, then with expected future short-term rates unchanged, greater interest rate volatility lowers spot rates through the convexity effect.

changes.from: has no impact on the term structure
changes.to: lowers spot rates through the convexity effect

statement: When expected short-term rates are flat and the tree reflects a risk premium and significant volatility, yields rise at the short end of the term structure but fall at the long end.
explanation: The risk premium grows roughly linearly with maturity, so it dominates at short maturities. The convexity effect grows roughly with the square of maturity and eventually overwhelms it, giving a humped curve.
originalText: In the shorter end, the yield increases, but in the longer end, the yield decreases

statement: With flat expected short-term rates and a volatile risk-neutral binomial tree, the term structure of spot rates is slightly downward sloping because of convexity.
explanation: With no risk premium, convexity is the only influence and averaging discount factors gives a higher price, hence a lower yield, at longer maturities.
originalText: Slightly downward sloping, since discounting the terminal cash flow over longer time periods when interest rates exhibit volatility results in slightly lower spot rates.

statement: When expected short-term rates and risk premiums are the same, long-dated spot rates in a higher-volatility market sit further below the expected short rate than in a lower-volatility market, and the gap widens with maturity.
explanation: Only the convexity effect differs. It always lowers yields and is larger with higher volatility and longer maturity.
originalText: Market A’s long‑dated spot rates will sit further below the expected short rate than Market B’s, and the gap will widen with maturity in both markets.

statement: As the maturity of a zero-coupon bond increases, all else equal, its price-yield curve becomes more convex.
explanation: The value of convexity rises with maturity (for example about 1.84 bp for a 2-year zero and about 5 bp for a 3-year zero).
originalText: more convex.

statement: If investors are risk neutral (zero risk premium), the expected one-year return on a zero-coupon bond equals the short-term rate regardless of its maturity or duration.
explanation: Expected return equals r0 plus lambda times duration, and lambda is zero. Convexity does not create an expected excess return.
originalText: It is the same: both have an expected return equal to the short‑term rate $r_{0}$.

statement: If investors are risk neutral, the greater convexity of a longer-maturity zero-coupon bond earns it a higher expected return than a shorter-maturity zero-coupon bond.
explanation: Convexity raises the return component but lowers the forward rate by the same amount, so the net expected return is unchanged and equals the short-term rate.
originalText: It is higher, because the 10‑year bond has greater convexity that earns extra return from rate volatility.

statement: The forward rate increases with the expected change in the short-term rate, scaled by the bond's duration.
explanation: The expectations term in the forward rate decomposition is the expected change in the short rate multiplied by duration.
originalText: The forward rate increases with the expected change in the short‑term rate, scaled by the bond’s duration.

statement: The forward rate increases with the risk premium in proportion to the bond's duration.
explanation: The risk premium term in the decomposition is lambda times duration.
originalText: The forward rate increases with the risk premium in proportion to duration.

statement: Greater interest rate volatility lowers the forward rate through the convexity effect.
explanation: The convexity effect is subtracted in the forward rate decomposition and grows with volatility.

statement: Because convexity raises a bond's return, it also raises the forward rate, so greater volatility steepens the forward curve.
explanation: Convexity enters the forward rate with a negative sign, so greater volatility lowers forward rates rather than raising them.
originalText: Because convexity raises a bond’s return, it also raises the forward rate, so greater volatility steepens the forward curve.

statement: The risk premium component in the decomposition of forward rates is the compensation investors demand for bearing interest rate risk.
explanation: Risk-averse investors require extra return proportional to duration for bearing interest rate risk, and that extra return is the risk premium.
originalText: The compensation investors demand for bearing interest rate risk.

statement: The risk premium component in the decomposition of forward rates is the compensation investors demand for convexity effects.
explanation: Convexity is a separate component, a Jensen's inequality effect of rate volatility. The risk premium is the compensation for bearing interest rate risk.
originalText: The compensation investors demand for convexity effects.
correction: The risk premium component in the decomposition of forward rates is the compensation investors demand for bearing interest rate risk.

statement: Forcing negative rates in a short-rate tree to zero changes the original distribution only where rates are very low, leaving rates away from zero unchanged.
explanation: Only nodes that would otherwise be negative are reset to zero, so the distribution is altered only in a very low rate environment. This is why the method may be preferred to switching to a non-negative distribution.
originalText: It changes the original distribution only where rates are very low, leaving rates away from zero unchanged.

statement: Forcing negative rates in a short-rate tree to zero introduces skewness and inappropriate volatilities across the entire distribution of rates.
explanation: Skewness and inappropriate volatilities are drawbacks attached to non-negative distributions such as the lognormal, which reshape the whole distribution. Flooring at zero alters only the nodes that would be negative.
originalText: It introduces skewness and inappropriate volatilities across the entire distribution of rates.

statement: Using a lognormal distribution for the short rate avoids negative short-term rates in a term structure model.
explanation: Lognormal rates cannot be negative, although this comes at the cost of skewness and inappropriate volatilities.
originalText: Using a lognormal distribution for the short rate.

statement: Adjusting an interest rate tree so that any negative rate is set to zero avoids negative short-term rates in the model.
explanation: Flooring negative tree rates at zero is a valid remedy and changes the distribution only at very low rates.
originalText: Adjusting the interest rate tree so that any negative rate is set to zero.

statement: Increasing the number of time steps so that the terminal distribution approaches a continuous normal distribution avoids negative short-term rates in a normally distributed short-rate model.
explanation: A finer tree converges to a normal distribution, which still assigns positive probability to negative rates. It is not a remedy.
originalText: Increasing the number of time steps so the terminal distribution approaches a continuous normal distribution.

statement: Negative short-term rates are a drawback of normally distributed rate models because investors can hold cash and earn a zero rate, so lending at a materially negative rate makes little economic sense.
explanation: Cash offers a zero return, so no one would lend at a materially negative rate. A model that generates such rates is economically unrealistic.
originalText: Investors can instead hold cash and earn a zero rate, so lending at a materially negative rate makes little economic sense.

statement: The problem of negative rates in a normally distributed short-rate model becomes smaller as the investment horizon lengthens.
explanation: Negative rates become more likely as the horizon lengthens, because the terminal distribution widens, and when the current rate is low.
originalText: Negative rates occur only for short horizons, so the problem is smaller as the investment horizon lengthens.
correction: The problem of negative rates in a normally distributed short-rate model becomes larger as the investment horizon lengthens.

statement: The conditional coverage statistic adds Kupiec's unconditional coverage statistic to Christoffersen's independence statistic and can reject a model even though its exception count is acceptable.
explanation: The joint test checks both the level of exceptions and whether they cluster. It catches a model whose exceptions are right in number but wrong in timing.
originalText: The conditional coverage statistic adds Kupiec’s $LR_{uc}$ to Christoffersen’s $LR_{ind}$ and can reject this model even though its exception count is acceptable.

statement: Kupiec's proportion of failures test rejects a model because its exceptions are bunched together in time.
explanation: Kupiec's test counts exceptions only and ignores their timing. Three clustered exceptions give the same failure rate as three spread-out ones, so clustering is detected by the independence test.
originalText: Kupiec’s proportion of failures test should reject the model, because exceptions bunched within two weeks raise the failure rate measured by the test.

statement: If a correct VaR model is rejected because of bad luck, the error committed is a Type 2 error.
explanation: Rejecting a correct model is a Type 1 error. A Type 2 error is failing to reject an incorrect model.
originalText: If the model is in fact correct and is rejected because of bad luck, the error committed is a Type 2 error, the risk that the Basel zones are designed to keep low.
correction: If a correct VaR model is rejected because of bad luck, the error committed is a Type 1 error.

statement: Christoffersen's independence test detects dependence between exceptions at any lag.
explanation: Christoffersen's test is a first-order Markov chain test, so it examines only whether an exception depends on the previous day's state. It does not detect dependence at longer distances.
originalText: Christoffersen’s independence test would also reject a model whose exceptions occur exactly one week apart, because it detects dependence between exceptions at any lag.
correction: Christoffersen's independence test detects dependence only between exceptions on consecutive days.

changes.from: detects dependence between exceptions at any lag
changes.to: detects dependence only between exceptions on consecutive days

statement: Principal mapping understates the true risk of a bond portfolio because it ignores the intervening coupon payments.
explanation: Principal mapping overstates the true risk because it maps the whole market value to the maturity of the principal and ignores intervening coupons. It gives the highest VaR of the three mapping methods.
originalText: Principal mapping understates the true risk of the portfolio, because it maps the market value to the average maturity of principal and ignores the intervening coupon payments.
correction: Principal mapping overstates the true risk of a bond portfolio because it ignores the intervening coupon payments.

statement: Duration mapping places the present value of each cash flow on the vertex nearest to its payment date.
explanation: That describes cash-flow mapping. Duration mapping replaces the whole portfolio by a single zero-coupon bond with maturity equal to the portfolio duration.
originalText: Duration mapping places the present value of each cash flow on the vertex nearest its payment date, which allows it to capture imperfect correlation along the curve.
correction: Cash-flow mapping places the present value of each cash flow on the vertex nearest to its payment date.

statement: Principal mapping and duration mapping, unlike cash-flow mapping, fail to preserve the market value of the portfolio.
explanation: All three mapping methods preserve market value. What separates cash-flow mapping is that it also preserves market risk more closely.
originalText: Cash-flow mapping is preferred because it preserves the market value of the portfolio, a property that principal mapping and duration mapping do not have.

statement: A VaR model fitted to a desk's historical actual P&L does not reflect the risk of the positions now held, so it would neither reveal the tail risk of short out-of-the-money option positions nor fall when positions are cut.
explanation: A short deep out-of-the-money put book earns small gains until the market moves, so its P&L history hides the tail risk. Only a VaR on the current positions shows the risk and responds to position changes.
originalText: The P&L history does not reflect the risk of the positions now held, so VaR would neither reveal the tail risk in the puts nor fall when positions are cut.

statement: A GARCH(1,1) model fitted to a desk's daily P&L cannot capture volatility clustering.
explanation: GARCH is designed to capture volatility clustering. The weakness of a VaR fitted to actual P&L is that the history does not reflect the positions currently held.
originalText: A GARCH model fitted to actual P&L cannot respond to volatility clustering, so the reported VaR is too stable over time.
correction: A GARCH(1,1) model fitted to a desk's daily P&L is designed to capture volatility clustering.

statement: Berkowitz and O'Brien found that a GARCH model fitted to banks' actual P&L was less accurate than banks' own VaR models.
explanation: Berkowitz and O'Brien found the GARCH model on actual P&L was more accurate than the banks' VaR models. The concern is conceptual soundness for the positions held, not accuracy.
originalText: A P&L-based GARCH VaR is known to be less accurate than banks’ positional VaR models, so it would fail a backtest.
correction: Berkowitz and O'Brien found that a GARCH model fitted to banks' actual P&L was more accurate than banks' own VaR models.
